title: The Hour of the Call
mood: At the hour she used to call, Vexana watches one lit window across the city.

hero.alt: A small four-pointed star badge blazes with pale blue light.
hero.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana comic, page 28

segs.t: The tower had lost its roof long ago. Vexana stood on its top floor, where the stone broke off into the night, her staff in her hand.
Past the last ruins rose the dome, a faint shell of light over the city. In the girls’ wing, the one window was still lit.
It was the hour when she used to call.
Her hand went to her side for the phone. There was no pocket to find.
There had been one once, in a purple skirt. The skirt lay folded in the void with the rest of her uniform.

In the first weeks she had made the call from her own window, with the training hall lit across the grounds. One night Guinevere answered on the first ring. She was out of breath, and the hall’s echo rang behind her voice.
“Go to bed,” said Vexana.
“You say that every night.” A drone whirred somewhere near the phone. “Normal people say goodnight, you know.”
“Go to bed.”
“That’s not goodnight.”
“It is.”
The line went silent. Then Guinevere laughed so loudly that Vexana held the phone away from her ear.
“Fine. Goodnight to you too, Vexana.”
Across the grounds the hall went dark, one row of windows after another. Vexana watched until the last row went out. Then she went to bed herself.
Tonight the window in the girls’ wing stayed lit past the hour.
She’ll be at her bench,
Vexana thought.
A drone open under the lamp. Soldering until dawn.
From here she could not see past the glass.
A wind came off the dead ground. The star blades at her shoulders turned in it.
“Go to bed,” she whispered.
The light did not change.
It is goodnight,
she thought.
You know it is.
She waited. The wind moved in the broken stone around her feet.
Her hand had gone back to her side. It closed on nothing.
At her right wrist, inside her sleeve, the star glowed. It had been lit since the first hour. It was lit now.
She felt its warmth through the cloth and turned the wrist in against her cloak.
One word at the gate,
she thought,
and she’d be over the fence by morning. Both drones. No pass.
The star tells her I’m alive. Let it be the one true thing she gets from me.
“For the sake of the Aspirant spirit, I will lie,” she told the window.
That night the window never went dark.
Vexana stayed. The stars over the dead ground thinned and went out. Over the bay the sky turned gray, and the lamps along the shore went out one by one.
Behind her the dark opened. Its cold touched the back of her neck: the door, come to take her back.
She did not move.
A little longer.
In the gray, the window was only a pale square in a pale wall. Soon she could not tell if its lamp was still lit, or if it was only morning on the glass.
Then she turned and went through.
Some nights later an errand brought her past the tower again. The feeders were far out in the dead ground, tearing cable out of an old pumping station. She climbed the tower alone.
It was the old hour. The girls’ wing was dark, every window.
Her grip tightened on the staff.
She went to bed,
she thought.
Good.
Then she saw the other light.
At the top of the Academy’s tower, under the beam, sat the glass room of the observation lab. Vexana had never seen a light up there at night. Tonight a lamp burned in it.
A long dark shape lay across the lit glass, one end raised toward the bay.
She watched it. After a while it had moved, its end turned farther along the sky.
A telescope. Somebody was searching the sky with it, one piece at a time.
It pointed out over the bay. On the far side of that sky hung the crack Vexana measured with her thumb. From the city, nothing showed there yet.
She knew only one girl who would search a whole sky by hand and call it a plan.
She’s looking for me.
Guinevere had come after her once before. On Team-Up Day she had crossed the courtyard in six strides. “Be my partner!”
“No,” Vexana had said.
Guinevere asked again the next day, on the stairs. She kept asking until the answer changed. She never once wavered.
But she had not known where it led. To a corridor and a claw. To a telescope at the top of a tower, all night, for someone who would not come.
“If we could start over, would she waver?” Vexana asked the dark.
Across the city the telescope turned a little farther along the sky.
Her weight had gone onto her front foot, toward the broken edge. She took it back.
From here no star could beep, and she meant to keep it that way.
Long before dawn the door opened behind her.
She did not turn around. She stepped back into it, her eyes on the lit glass at the top of the tower, until the dark closed over it.
